rv.q: This entire revitalized gothic romance with its 1980s guitar riffs has that invigorating effect.
Perhaps even more surprising is that, somehow, they pull it off.
There’s only so much you can “elevate” about a work that fundamentally wants to revel in some schlocky mud.
Masquerade is a lot of fun if you're in the right mood.

The result sort of resembles Frankenstein’s monster, but it works exceedingly well. There’s plenty of pomp and circumstance involved in seeing it. You’re asked to wear formal attire in black, white, or silver only.

As directed by Diane Paulus, the performances are seldom subtle, especially at close quarters, but the cast brings the requisite heat and vocal stamina for Lloyd Webber’s strenuous score, sung to pre-recorded instrumental tracks.
You can either stage “Phantom” in a theater or create a non-narrative funhouse party experience, but trying to do both at once satisfies neither.

The result of this world creation is a truly moving, unforgettable experience that takes you to the darkest depths of the human mind; yet it still provides hope for a brighter future filled with music and light.
Paulus and team have pulled off something miraculous: an immersive evening that retains the essence and dramatic arc of its source material.

cn.t: This immersive reimagining of "Phantom of the Opera" divides critics, who praise its ambitious spectacle and intimate staging but question whether the gimmickry enhances or distracts from the beloved musical.
